question: Which statement best describes The basic shape: { [K in keyof T]: T[K] }?
options: A mapped type iterates over the union of keys produced by keyof T, binding each one to K, and produces a property for each. { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } is the identity transform — it reproduces T. Everything else is a variation on this skeleton: change the modifiers, change the value type, or remap the key.

The minus prefix strips a modifier that already exists on the source type. -readonly removes immutability and -? makes optional properties required. This is how Required<T> ({ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }) and Mutable<T> are built — they reverse what Partial/Readonly add.

The right-hand side can be any type expression, not just T[K]. You can wrap each value: { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null } makes every field nullable; { [K in keyof T]: () => T[K] } turns each value into a getter. This is where mapped types become powerful — uniform value transforms across an entire shape.

You can attach readonly and/or ? in front of the value to make every property read-only or optional. type Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] } makes all properties optional; type Readonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] } makes them immutable. The modifier applies uniformly to every mapped property.

TypeScript 4.1+ lets you rewrite keys using an `as` clause: { [K in keyof T as NewKey]: T[K] }. Combined with template literal types you can prefix keys (`get${Capitalize<...>}`) or, by mapping a key to never, filter it out entirely. This turns mapped types into key transformers, not just value transformers.
